# `gcp.healthcheck`

Health Checks determine whether instances are responsive and able to do work. They are an important part of a comprehensive load balancing configuration, as they enable monitoring instances behind load balancers. Health Checks poll instances at a specified interval. Instances that do not respond successfully to some number of probes in a row are marked as unhealthy. No new connections are sent to unhealthy instances, though existing connections will continue. The health check will continue to poll unhealthy instances. If an instance later responds successfully to some number of consecutive probes, it is marked healthy again and can receive new connections. ~>**NOTE**: Legacy HTTP(S) health checks must be used for target pool-based network load balancers. See the \[official guide\](https://cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/health-check-concepts#selecting_hc) for choosing a type of health check.

| Tier | 1 (ruled: One hook, doing two convenience jobs, both of which this provider asks the user to do explicitly instead.
encoder (encoders/health_check_type.tmpl) looks at which of the seven per-protocol blocks the configuration set -- http, https, http2, tcp, ssl, grpc, grpc_tls -- and from that DERIVES the required top-level `type` field. It also defaults the nested `port` to 80 or 443 when neither a port nor a port_name was given.
`type` is an ordinary settable enum on the compute v1 HealthCheck message (checked against the Discovery document: not readOnly, enum GRPC, GRPC_WITH_TLS, HTTP, HTTP2, HTTPS, INVALID, SSL, TCP), so this provider exposes it directly and the user writes it. The port defaults the hook applies are the API's OWN documented defaults -- compute's HTTPHealthCheck says "The default value is 80" in the Discovery document itself -- so omitting the port leaves Google applying the same number the hook would have sent.
THE BOUNDED GAP: `type` must be set in configuration. Terraform infers it; we do not. magic-modules marks `type` output because the encoder derives it, and until 2026-09-24 the generator obeyed that, so the one field Google requires could not be written and every health check create failed. `settable` and `required` above make it the user's. Omitting it produces Google's own required-field error at create time, which is loud and names the field. Inferring it would mean the generator writing per-resource Go, which is the thing the tier gate exists to keep out.
Needed for any load balancer: backend services reference health checks.
